Sure. The first thing we did was go stand on the floor. You can't really assess a task like that from a spreadsheet or a process document, because the documented process and what people actually do on the line are almost never the same thing. So we spent time watching the operators, filming the cycles, and talking to the folks who'd been doing the job for years about where it gets tricky.

From there we broke the work down into its pieces. Where are the parts coming from: totes, racks, a conveyor? How consistent is their position and orientation when they arrive? What's the weight range, what are the materials, are there any reflective or deformable parts that make perception harder? Then on the other side: where does the part need to go, and how precise does that placement have to be? A lot of suitability comes down to tolerances. If the next station needs a part within a couple of millimeters and the incoming presentation is pretty chaotic, that's a very different problem than loose placement into a bin.

We also looked hard at cycle time and variability. It's not enough for the robot to do the task once in a demo. It has to hit the takt time, shift after shift, and recover gracefully when something unexpected happens, like a part that's flipped, a tote that's slightly out of place, or a person walking through the cell. So we asked: what are the edge cases, how often do they happen, and what does a human do today when they hit one?

Then there's the integration side, which people tend to underestimate. What's the footprint? Do we need to change any fixtures or the layout? How does the robot get signals from the line? What are the safety requirements in that zone? Sometimes a task is technically doable but the changes to the surrounding environment make it not worth it.

And finally, the economics and the people. Is this a job that's hard to staff, or ergonomically tough, repetitive lifting, awkward reaches? Those are usually the best places to start, because the plant genuinely wants relief there and the operators are happy to hand it off. Once all of that lined up, we ran it in a mock-up cell with real parts before ever going live, so by the time we were on the actual line there weren't many surprises.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The first thing we did was spend time on the floor, not in a conference room. You can't assess parts handling from a spec sheet. We watched the actual stations for a couple of days: how parts arrived, how they were oriented, how often something showed up damaged or out of place, what the operators did when things went wrong. That last part matters a lot. The exceptions tell you more about whether a job is a fit than the nominal process does.

Then we broke it down along a few dimensions. One was variability in the parts themselves. If every part is the same shape and comes in a fixed fixture, that's easy, and honestly a traditional industrial arm might do it cheaper. If there's a mix of part geometries, or they come in loose in bins, or the presentation changes shift to shift, that's where a more general-purpose robot earns its keep. Georgia was somewhere in the middle, which was actually a good sign for us.

The second dimension was the physical envelope. Reach, payload, how much the robot has to move around versus work in one place, whether it has to share space with people. We did fairly careful measurements of the heaviest and most awkward parts, because a job that's 95 percent within spec and 5 percent outside it is a job you can't fully automate, and then the economics change.

And the third thing, which people underestimate, was the upstream and downstream dependencies. The robot might handle the part fine, but if the conveyor timing is inconsistent, or the tote it's loading into gets swapped for a different one on second shift, you inherit all of that. So we worked with the plant team to map out what would have to be standardized around the robot, and whether they were willing to do that.

We ran a short pilot on one cell before committing to anything broader. We set clear metrics ahead of time, mostly cycle time, pick success rate, and how many interventions per shift an operator had to make. If we couldn't hit those in the pilot, we weren't going to pretend scaling would fix it. It turned out two of the stations were a great fit, one needed some fixturing changes, and one we told them frankly wasn't worth automating yet. Being willing to say no on that last one is probably what made them trust us on the other three.

The key question was whether this was a repeatable process or something that required a person to make a new judgment every time. Then we looked at the exceptions—what happens when a part is out of position or something doesn’t go as expected. That’s what determines whether you can make the whole process reliable, rather than just demonstrate a successful pick.

sol-6.1.text:
We started by watching the people doing the job and breaking it down into individual steps. Where are the parts coming from? How consistently are they presented? How heavy are they, and where do they need to go? Something that looks simple to a person can be quite challenging for a robot, especially if the parts arrive in different orientations.

Then we looked at whether we could do it reliably at the pace the factory needed. Picking up a part once is a demonstration; doing it over and over through a production shift is the actual job. And finally, the economics had to make sense. Could we take a repetitive task off somebody’s plate and deliver enough value to justify putting the robot there?
